faq: Why not just use a general AI assistant?
For one-off questions, do. A system is for the work that keeps coming back: it's connected to your email, documents and calendar, runs on its own schedule and is built around how you do the job.
Is my job a good fit?

If information arrives all the time, there's a lot to keep track of, or you write the same kind of reply again and again, probably yes. Tell us about it and we'll say plainly whether a system would help.
Do I need to be technical?
No. You tell us how the work happens in your own words. We design it, build it, test it and set it up where you already work.
Where does my information live?
Wherever you're comfortable: on your own computer, on a private server we run just for you, or in your own accounts. We agree on it before anything is built.
Can it do something I didn't want?
Only what you allow. It can be read-only, ask before it sends anything, and keep a record of every change it makes so it can be undone.
What can it connect to?
Most of what your work already runs on: email, texts, calendars, shared folders, spreadsheets, websites and many online services. If something has no way in, we'll tell you before we start.
What if my customers or employees don't speak the same language as me?

It tells you what they said in your language and writes your reply back in theirs. Before anything goes out, a separate check confirms every number, date and instruction came through exactly. If it can't confirm one, the message waits and you're told why, in your language.
Does it have to be an app?
No. It can be a message on your phone each morning, a website, a private dashboard, an iPhone app, or a mix of them.
How much does it do on its own?
As much or as little as you like. Some people want drafts to approve; others want jobs handled start to finish. You choose, and you can change it later.
What does it cost?
It depends on what the system does. Tell us the idea and we'll come back with a plan and a price. You pay nothing until you decide to go ahead with a build.
What happens once it's built?
It keeps working for you, and we can keep extending it as your needs change.

qa.title: AI-built. Not AI slop.
qa.lede: Software thrown together with AI has earned a reputation for looking fine and falling apart. Ours goes through strict testing and review before it reaches you, because the experience is the product.
points: Nothing counts as done until it has been run and checked on screen. Passing tests alone don't prove it works.
Reviewers from three different AI companies judge the experience the way a newcomer would: is it clear at a glance, and would you show it to a friend? It doesn't ship without a pass.
Automated tests run against real databases, real browsers and simulated iPhones, and they have to pass before anything ships.
The code is reviewed line by line, the way a careful colleague would, before anything goes out.
When something misses its target, nobody moves the goalposts or calls it close enough. It gets fixed.
Known issues get fixed, not shipped
Anything spotted before launch is fixed first, even small cosmetic things.

steps: Tell us the idea
A sentence is enough: the thing you keep losing track of, the job that eats your evenings, the question you wish you could just ask.
We map how the work happens
Where information arrives, what decisions you make, who else is involved and what a great result looks like to you.
You decide what it handles
What it does on its own, what it checks with you first and how it reaches you. It's your system, set up your way.
We build it and switch it on
You see it working on your real day-to-day, then it grows one piece at a time as your needs do.

build.title: What we can build
build.lede: Our five systems use only part of what's possible. These are the building blocks for yours, including some our own systems haven't needed yet.
blocks: A natural-sounding voice picks up every call, day or night, answers the common questions and books the job.
Texts, email and website chat answered in your tone and in your customer's language, with anything tricky handed to you.
Appointments scheduled, confirmed and moved, with reminders so fewer people forget.
Invoices, receipts, forms and contracts read, filed and entered where they belong.
Quotes drafted, invoices sent and late payments followed up politely.
Prices, reviews, permits, deadlines and the news that matters to you, checked every day.
Sales, bookings and spending pulled into one short daily report or a live dashboard.
Replies, posts, newsletters and listings drafted in your voice, ready for your OK.
build.tools: It works with what you already use: Google or Microsoft email and calendars, spreadsheets, accounting and online-shop tools, and many more.

cases_lede: Each one started as a single sentence about a job. Here's what they do now.

stories.title: The repair that turned out to be free
stories.moment: At 11 pm a tenant emails: the dishwasher leaked and the kitchen floor feels soft.

trail.text: Reads the message and the photo, and marks it urgent: water near a floor.
Finds the clause that makes appliance repairs the owner's job.
Notices the same dishwasher was fixed six weeks ago, and the plumber guarantees his work for 90 days.
A reply to the tenant, a note to the owner and a request to the same plumber under his guarantee.

stories.notify: Unit 4B leak: same plumber, covered by his 90-day guarantee. Three drafts ready for your OK.
stories.result: A repair that would have cost a few hundred dollars costs nothing, and the tenant hears back first thing in the morning.

stories.title: The permit that didn't lapse
stories.moment: Three jobs are running, and one permit is close to expiring before its final inspection.

trail.text: Checks every open permit overnight and sees one expires on the 20th.
The final inspection is booked for the 23rd, three days too late.
Finds an unread message from the inspector's office offering an earlier slot on the 17th.
A reply taking the earlier slot, and a line on that job's to-do list.

stories.notify: Oak St permit expires the 20th. Inspector offered the 17th; reply drafted.
stories.result: The inspection moves up, the permit stays valid, and nobody pays to re-file.

stories.title: The headcount that was six too high
stories.moment: The caterer needs a final number by Friday. Replies came in by form, by email and by text.

trail.text: Pulls in every form response.
Adds the guests who replied there instead, including two who never used the form.
Spots six guests who replied twice under slightly different names, and counts each once.
Drafts the final count with dietary needs: 9 vegetarian, 2 nut allergies.

stories.notify: Final headcount: 112, with 6 duplicates removed. Caterer email ready.
stories.result: You pay for 112 meals, not 118, and both allergies are on the caterer's sheet.

stories.title: The offer that came in during dinner
stories.moment: Saturday evening, an offer lands on one of your listings while you're out with family.

trail.text: Reads the offer and pulls out the price, closing date and conditions.
Checks them against what your sellers said matters most.
Flags the inspection period: 14 days, when your sellers wanted 7 at most.
A one-page summary for the sellers with a suggested counter.

stories.notify: Offer on Maple Ave: price works, inspection period too long (14 vs 7). Summary and counter drafted.
stories.result: You finish dinner. Sunday morning you call your sellers with a counter already written.

stories.title: Restocked before it sold out
stories.moment: Overnight, one product starts selling three times faster than usual.

trail.text: Spots the jump in sales before you're awake.
Works out that at this pace it sells out in four days.
Finds your supplier usually takes ten days to deliver.
A reorder email to the supplier, and a note to ease off the ads for that product until it arrives.

stories.notify: Linen tote selling 3× normal: out in about 4 days, supplier needs about 10. Reorder drafted.
stories.result: The reorder goes out on day one instead of the day it sells out.

stories.title: The form buried in a newsletter
stories.moment: The school's weekly newsletter mentions a field trip form due Friday, in its sixth paragraph.

trail.text: Reads the newsletter and pulls out the one thing with a deadline.
Sees you're traveling Thursday and Friday.
Finds your partner's reply on the school thread: they'll handle school things this week.
Puts the form on your partner's list for Wednesday evening, attached.

stories.notify: Field trip form due Friday. You're away, so it's on your partner's list for Wednesday.
stories.result: The form goes in on time, and nobody had to read the newsletter.

stories.title: A receptionist that never misses a call
stories.moment: It's 7 pm, you're under a sink, and the phone rings for the third time. Every call that goes to voicemail can be a job that goes to someone else.
stories.result: Every call is answered, nights and weekends included. The job is booked before you've packed up your tools, and urgent calls come straight through to you.
call: Hi, my water heater's leaking. Can someone come out today?
Sorry to hear that. I can get a technician to you between 2 and 4 tomorrow afternoon. What's the address?
14 Oak Street. Do you replace them too?
We do. The technician can price a replacement on site. You're booked for 2 to 4, and you'll get a text when they're on the way.
stories.notify: New job, tomorrow 2–4 pm: leaking water heater at 14 Oak St. Asked about a replacement.
